paragraphes: Passionate about animals and manual therapies for as long as I can remember, I naturally turned towards studies in animal osteopathy.

After five years of training and my registration on the National Register of Competence held by the CNOV, I settled in the Toulouse region, where I am originally from, in order to practise there from 2020 onwards.
Sport, and athletics in particular, has held an important place in my journey. It instilled in me values of rigour, perseverance and discipline that continue to guide my professional practice today.
Committed to supporting the development and recognition of animal osteopathy in France, I was involved for several years within associations working towards the structuring of the profession.

From 2017 to 2020, I served as President of the Union Française des Étudiants Ostéopathes Animaliers (UFEOA), before co-founding the Collectif des Ostéopathes Animaliers, within which I remained actively involved from 2020 to 2025. This has since become the national union representing professionals registered on the RNA held by the CNOV.

Driven by a desire to create connections between the various stakeholders in animal health, I initiated the organisation of the SymbiOsteo conferences in 2019 and 2022, and later co-created the SymbiOsteo podcast in 2024. These projects aim to foster exchanges between veterinarians practising osteopathy, animal osteopaths and human osteopaths, whilst highlighting developments in practice, current affairs and research prospects in this field.

In 2025, I wished to deepen my knowledge and develop an approach more oriented towards scientific research. I therefore enrolled in the Master 2 'Gestion des Établissements de Formation et de Recherche en Santé' at the Université de Haute-Alsace in Mulhouse. This training led to my first scientific publication in the integrative health journal Hegel: 'Ostéopathie, chiropraxie, thérapies manuelles: analyse bibliométrique (1949–2025)'.

liste.titre: Case history — gathering information on your animal's health and creating your file
paragraphes: Each consultation begins with a discussion to gather the essential information about your animal and the reason for the osteopathy session. Its medical history, lifestyle, behaviour, diet, activity and environment are all discussed in order to gain a comprehensive view of its situation.
This step allows your osteopath to place the animal within its living context and to tailor the clinical and osteopathic examination accordingly.
Your animal's file is then created and securely stored via Djooka, the digital health record dedicated to animals. You will find the consultation reports as well as the associated invoices there.
The consultation continues with a dynamic and static observation of your animal.

The analysis of locomotion allows the quality of movement, the symmetry of gaits and the range of motion to be assessed, as well as identifying any restrictions in mobility, compensations or gait irregularities.
The static observation complements this examination by looking for any postural imbalances, weight shifting, pain-related postures or bodily adaptations that may indicate functional discomfort.
A thorough palpatory examination is then carried out to confirm that your animal is indeed suitable for osteopathic care.

This step helps identify any warning signs requiring prior or complementary referral to your veterinarian. Osteopathy is always practised within the scope of its competence and as a complement to veterinary follow-up when this is indicated.
Using a precise manual examination, the osteopath assesses the mobility of the joints, muscles, fasciae, viscera, skull and various tissues of the body.
This overall assessment helps identify restrictions in mobility, functional adaptations and compensations that may contribute to the imbalances observed.
A summary is then presented and explained to you before the osteopathic treatment is carried out.
Treatment relies exclusively on manual techniques adapted to each animal, its species, age, activity and the reason for the consultation.
The aim is to restore optimal tissue mobility, improve the quality of movement, support the body's capacity for adaptation and contribute to the animal's functional comfort.
My practice draws on various complementary approaches: musculoskeletal, myofascial, tissue-based, visceral, fluid-based, cranial, reflex and tensegrity-based.
At the end of the session, you will receive a report along with personalised recommendations tailored to your animal's needs.
This advice covers, among other things, rest management, the gradual resumption of activity, any recommended exercises, as well as points to watch for in the days following the consultation.
The aim is to promote optimal recovery and to place the care within an overall health and well-being approach, in collaboration with your veterinarian where necessary.

paragraphes: Animal osteopathy developed in France from the 1980s onwards. Initially applied to equines, it was adapted by veterinary surgeon Dominique Giniaux and human osteopath Pascal Evrard, who greatly contributed to its growth within the equestrian world.
In the early 2000s, this discipline gradually extended to companion animals, notably thanks to the work of veterinary surgeon Francis Lizon.
A few years later, its development continued in the livestock sector, particularly driven by veterinary surgeon Jean-Pierre Siméon, a pioneer of bovine osteopathy in France.
Animal osteopathy is practised on many species: companion animals, horses, livestock, but also sporting, working or performance animals.

Over recent decades, complementary approaches to animal health have grown considerably. More and more owners wish to incorporate manual therapies into their animals' medical care, as part of a comprehensive approach to prevention, comfort and well-being.
Thanks to its exclusively manual approach, it provides a comprehensive functional assessment of the animal, focusing on the interactions between the body's different systems.

histoire.synthese: Animal osteopathy is a so-called natural integrative medicine: through its manual approach, it offers a different and complementary overall perspective to veterinary medicine.

paragraphes: Through this aspect of osteopathy, we work to rebalance the structure. This may involve techniques known as structural, myotensive or functional; either direct or indirect.

liste.alt: Marie Salabert mobilising a German shepherd's hindquarters
paragraphes: These techniques can be applied across the whole body. They aim to improve the movement of a targeted structure or, more broadly, to restore good tissue communication from one end of the body to the other.

liste.alt: Hands laid flat along the back of a seated German shepherd
paragraphes: The body is largely composed of fascia, initially described as mesoderm at the embryological stage. During the development of the embryo and foetus, this mesoderm differentiates into several types of fascia: superficial (dermis - hypodermis); intermediate (aponeuroses, serous membranes and splanchnic mesos, vessel sheaths); and deep (periosteum, tendons, dura mater).
In recent years, fascia has been the subject of much scientific research, and it fascinates osteopaths just as much.

liste.alt: A hand supporting a foal's foreleg, in close-up
paragraphes: We focus on the mobility of organs and their ligamentous attachments. My final dissertation notably examined the practice of osteopathy on the means of fixation of the various organs.

liste.alt: Hands resting on a young dog's head and neck
paragraphes: Reflex techniques work locally on the skin to induce a deeper action within the body. I particularly enjoy performing drawn lines focused on certain areas, allowing for both a localised and overall action on the lymphatic, circulatory and nervous systems.

jalons.texte: The Ministry of Agriculture recognises the practice of animal osteopaths under section 12° of Article L243-3 of the Rural and Maritime Fishing Code (CRPM).

Animal osteopathy procedures may be carried out by non-veterinary practitioners who have passed the national aptitude test, are registered on the National Aptitude Register (RNA) and appear on the list maintained by the National Council of the Order of Veterinary Surgeons (CNOV).

legislation.obligation: Furthermore, animal osteopaths are required to refer owners to a veterinary surgeon when the animal's condition requires a medical diagnosis, treatment, or when the observed disorders fall outside the scope of osteopathy. This obligation is part of the code of ethics set out in the Rural Code.

rente.titre: Rural osteopathy for farm and production animals
rente.chapo: Animal osteopathy developed within the farming sector from the 2000s onwards. Historically, farmers in rural areas have always relied on traditional manual practices to support their animals through certain functional difficulties.
paragraphes: Today, animal osteopathy continues this tradition by offering a structured manual approach, suited to current animal welfare standards and complementary to veterinary care.

Having grown up in a rural environment, I was fortunate to spend time around various farm animals (dairy cattle, pigs, rabbits). This closeness to the farming world helped me understand the realities on the ground and the daily challenges faced by farmers.
Through animal osteopathy, the aim today is to contribute to the comfort of farm animals and support professionals in a comprehensive approach to animal welfare.

formation.question: How do you become an animal osteopath? Do you need to be a vet or a qualified osteopath (DO) beforehand?
formation.reponse: In France, it is not necessary to be a vet or a qualified human osteopath (DO) to practise animal osteopathy. Several training pathways lead to this profession, provided the current regulatory requirements are met, notably passing the national aptitude examination organised by the Conseil national de l'Ordre des vétérinaires (CNOV), which is essential for practising animal osteopathy as a non-veterinarian. Three main training routes exist: 1. Undertake specialised training in animal osteopathy — It is possible to enrol in a school of animal osteopathy, which generally offers a five-year course of study comprising theoretical, practical and clinical teaching. At the end of this training, the candidate must pass the CNOV's national aptitude examination in order to be authorised to practise animal osteopathy in France. 2. Train in human osteopathy and then specialise in animal osteopathy — Qualified human osteopaths may also supplement their training with specific instruction in animal osteopathy. They must, however, meet the regulatory requirements applicable to non-veterinarians and pass the CNOV's national aptitude examination. It is essential to choose a comprehensive course that covers the study of the various animal species and provides preparation suited to the requirements of the national examination. 3. Become a vet and then specialise in veterinary osteopathy — Veterinary students can train in animal osteopathy as part of a further specialisation, notably by obtaining an Inter-School Diploma (DIE) in veterinary osteopathy. This route allows the osteopathic approach to be integrated into a complete veterinary medical training.

formation.question: What are the main subjects taught in animal osteopathy?
formation.reponse: Training as an animal osteopath is based on multidisciplinary teaching combining scientific knowledge, an understanding of how animals function, and the learning of manual techniques. The main fundamental theoretical subjects include: Animal anatomy, to gain precise knowledge of the body's structures and their interactions; Physiology, to understand how the body's various systems function; Biomechanics and locomotion, essential for analysing movement and bodily adaptations; Veterinary semiology, enabling the identification of signs requiring referral to a vet. Other subjects complete the training: cell biology; biochemistry; histology; pathophysiology; animal husbandry; animal nutrition; ethology; animal welfare; ethics and professional conduct; public health. Practical training then enables students to master the various osteopathic approaches, notably musculoskeletal, fascial, tissue, visceral, cranial and other techniques adapted to the different species.

comprendre.question: Does an animal osteopathy consultation necessarily involve manipulations that make the joints "crack"?
comprendre.reponse: No. Contrary to certain preconceived ideas, an animal osteopathy consultation does not necessarily rely on manipulations involving joint sounds. Osteopathy uses various manual techniques suited to each animal, their age, species, state of health and sensitivity. The approaches may be articular, muscular, fascial, tissue-based, visceral or cranial, without any systematic aim to produce a "crack". The objective is not to force a movement, but to guide the tissues towards better mobility and more balanced functioning, always respecting the animal's comfort.

comprendre.question: From what age can an animal see an osteopath?
comprendre.reponse: Osteopathy is suited to animals of all ages. A consultation can be considered from the very first days of life, during growth, in adulthood or in senior animals, depending on their needs.

comprendre.question: Does my animal need a veterinary prescription?
comprendre.reponse: No. In France, an animal osteopath registered on the Registre National d'Aptitude (RNA) may see an animal without a veterinary prescription. However, should the animal's condition require it, they will always refer the owner to their vet.

comprendre.question: Does animal osteopathy replace veterinary medicine?
comprendre.reponse: No. Osteopathy is a complementary approach to veterinary care. It replaces neither a medical diagnosis nor veterinary treatment when this is required.

consultation.question: How does a consultation take place?
consultation.reponse: A consultation includes a discussion about your animal's history, a locomotor and postural examination, a palpatory examination, an osteopathic diagnosis, followed by an appropriate manual treatment. Personalised advice is then given to you to optimise your animal's recovery.

consultation.question: Are the manipulations painful?
consultation.reponse: The techniques used are adapted to each animal and their state of health. Some animals may show sensitivity in areas that are already painful, but the manipulations are carried out with respect for their comfort.

consultation.question: How long does a consultation last?
consultation.reponse: The average duration is 35 minutes to 1 hour, depending on the species, the reason for the consultation and the animal's needs.

consultation.question: How many sessions are needed?
consultation.reponse: Every animal is unique. A single session may sometimes be enough, while certain situations require regular follow-up. The number of consultations is determined according to the animal's progress and needs.

consultation.question: Does my animal need to rest after the session?
consultation.reponse: Yes. A period of rest is generally recommended for the 24 to 72 hours following the consultation, to allow the body to adapt to the changes brought about by the treatment. Appropriate recommendations will be given to you at the end of the session.

consultation.question: Can I have a preventive consultation?
consultation.reponse: Yes. Osteopathy can be part of preventive care throughout your animal's life, without any specific reason for consultation.

consultation.question: Should I bring anything to the consultation?
consultation.reponse: It is recommended to bring recent veterinary reports if your animal is being followed for a medical condition. For horses and farm animals, a secure space allowing them to be observed and handled is required. For cats, a towel or blanket on a table is preferred for their comfort and the practicality of the manipulations.

consultation.question: Are consultations reimbursed?
consultation.reponse: Some pet health insurance policies cover all or part of the cost of osteopathy consultations. Terms vary depending on the policy; it is advisable to check with your insurer. If needed, a treatment form will be completed.

consultation.question: When should you not consult an osteopath?
consultation.reponse: In the event of an emergency (fracture, significant wound, breathing difficulty, fever, suspected infection, neurological distress, etc.), it is essential to contact a veterinarian as a priority. Osteopathy may possibly be considered afterwards, as a complement to medical care.

consultation.question: Can the animal osteopath communicate directly with my vet?
consultation.reponse: Yes. Communication between the various professionals involved in caring for your animal allows for comprehensive and consistent care. With your agreement, the animal osteopath can communicate with your treating vet in order to share useful information for your animal's follow-up, while respecting each professional's role and expertise. Osteopathy is part of an approach that complements veterinary care, with the shared aim of promoting your animal's health, comfort, mobility and wellbeing.

consultation.question: Can I stay present during the osteopathy consultation?
consultation.reponse: Yes. Your presence is welcomed during the consultation. Your knowledge of the animal, its habits and behaviour is a valuable source of information during the case history and throughout the session. Your presence also allows you to take part in the discussion, understand the observations made and receive the advice needed to best support your animal after the consultation.

situations.question: My dog is wary or reactive: how does a session go in that situation?
situations.reponse: Dogs that are reactive or find handling difficult are animals I meet regularly in consultation. I am trained to adapt the session to each profile and to respect each animal's pace. To prepare the session as well as possible, we talk on the phone before I come. That lets me gather the important information about your dog and its usual reactions, and set up the best possible conditions for the meeting to go calmly. If you would like your dog to wear a muzzle to make the session safer, it can be used at your request. If your animal shows marked signs of wariness, fear or aggression, we will also adapt our respective attitudes and postures to foster a climate of trust and safety for everyone. My aim is always to respect your dog's limits. If it is genuinely not able to be approached or touched on the day, the session will not go ahead, so as not to reinforce its defensive reactions or its distrust of handling. In that case we will simply make sure the meeting ends on a positive, reassuring note before I leave.

situations.question: My dog is limping, can osteopathy help?
situations.reponse: Lameness can have many origins and sometimes requires a veterinary examination to identify its cause. Once the medical cause has been addressed, or when the situation relates to a functional disorder, osteopathy can help improve the animal's locomotor comfort. It allows the practitioner to assess the compensations the body has put in place, mobility restrictions and functional imbalances that may persist after a painful episode. The aim is to support a return to more harmonious locomotion and to limit the establishment of compensations, alongside veterinary follow-up where this is required.

situations.question: My horse is stiff or lacks suppleness, should I consult an osteopath?
situations.reponse: A decrease in suppleness, stiffness or a change in locomotion can be linked to various causes: constraints related to work, postural adaptations, discomfort, ageing or functional compensations. An osteopathy consultation allows the practitioner to assess the horse's overall mobility, its bodily balance and any restrictions that may be limiting its comfort or physical capacities. In both sport horses and leisure horses, the aim is to encourage fluid locomotion, better adaptation to physical demands and optimal comfort.

situations.question: My animal's behaviour has changed, could an osteopathy consultation help?
situations.reponse: A change in behaviour can have many origins: environment, upbringing, stress, pain or physical discomfort. When bodily discomfort contributes to a change in behaviour, osteopathy can help identify certain functional restrictions that may be affecting the animal's wellbeing. It can be part of a multidisciplinary approach, working alongside the vet, veterinary behaviourist or specialist trainer where necessary.

situations.question: When should you consult an osteopath for a sporting animal?
situations.reponse: Sporting animals are subject to significant physical demands requiring appropriate monitoring. A consultation may be considered: in preparation for a sporting season or a period of intense activity; before an important event; after sustained effort, to support recovery; in the event of a drop in performance or a change in locomotion; and as a preventive measure, to monitor compensations linked to training.

paragraphes: Our website, {{site.url}} (hereinafter: "the website") uses cookies and other related technologies (for simplicity, all these technologies are referred to as "cookies"). No cookies are placed by third parties without your prior consent. In the document below, we inform you about the use of cookies on our website.

A cookie is a small, simple file sent along with the pages of this website and stored by your browser on the hard drive of your computer or another device. The information stored therein may be returned to our servers or to the servers of the relevant third parties during a subsequent visit.
A script is a piece of code used to ensure that our website functions properly and interactively. This code is executed on our server or on your device.

A web beacon (or tracking pixel) is a small, invisible piece of text or image on a website used to monitor traffic on that website. To do this, various pieces of data about you are stored using web beacons. Our website does not use web beacons.

Certain cookies ensure that particular parts of the website function properly and that your preferences as a user are taken into account. By placing functional cookies, we make it easier for you to visit our website: you will not need to repeatedly enter the same information when visiting our website. We may place these cookies without your consent.

Marketing/tracking cookies are cookies or any other form of local storage used to build user profiles in order to display advertisements or to track a user on this website or across multiple websites for similar marketing purposes. Our website does not place any marketing or tracking cookies, and does not use any audience measurement tools.
The table below summarises all the cookies and data stored on your device by our website.
The site's contact form does not place any cookies: the information you enter there is sent to us by email and is used only to respond to your enquiry.

When you visit our website for the first time, we display a banner with an explanation about cookies. As soon as you click "Accept", you authorise us to load the third-party content described in this cookie policy. If you click "Decline", no third-party content is loaded and the site remains fully usable. Your choice is stored on your device and is not shared with anyone.

You can use your internet browser to automatically or manually delete cookies. You can also specify that certain cookies may not be placed. Another option is to change the settings of your internet browser so that you receive a message every time a cookie is placed. For more information about these options, please refer to the instructions in your browser's Help section.
If you delete your browsing data in your browser, your consent choice will be erased: the banner will be shown to you again on your next visit.
You have the following rights regarding your personal data:

To exercise these rights, please contact us. Please refer to the contact details at the bottom of this cookie policy. If you have a complaint about the way we handle your data, we would like to be informed of this, but you also have the right to lodge a complaint with the supervisory authority (the data protection authority).
You can also consult our privacy policy.
liste: You have the right to know why your personal data is needed, what will happen to it, and how long it will be retained.
Right of access: you have the right to access the personal data we hold about you.
Right of rectification: you have the right at any time to complete, correct, have deleted, or have blocked your personal data.
If you have given us your consent to process your data, you have the right to withdraw that consent and to have your personal data deleted.
Right to data portability: you have the right to request all your personal data from the data controller and to transfer it in full to another data controller.
Right to object: you may object to the processing of your data. We will comply, unless there are legitimate grounds for the processing.
